title: CT-defined sarcopenia and outcomes in HR+/HER2- metastatic breast cancer treated with CDK4/6 inhibitors.
abstract: Background Sarcopenia is increasingly recognized as a potential prognostic factor in patients with cancer, but its clinical significance in HR+/HER2- metastatic breast cancer treated with CDK4/6 inhibitors remains uncertain. This study investigated the association between CT-defined sarcopenia and clinical outcomes in this population. Methods This retrospective multicenter study included 94 patients with HR+/HER2- metastatic breast cancer who received ribociclib or palbociclib plus endocrine therapy between January 2021 and March 2024. Baseline sarcopenia was defined using the skeletal muscle index measured on CT at the third lumbar vertebral level (L3). Progression-free survival (PFS) was estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method. Cox proportional hazards regression was used to identify prognostic factors for PFS, with CT-defined sarcopenia, continuous skeletal muscle index (SMI), and total muscle area (TMA) evaluated in separate multivariable models. Results CT-defined sarcopenia was present in 37 patients (39.4%). Median PFS was markedly shorter in patients with sarcopenia than in those without sarcopenia (15.2 vs. 26.6 months; log-rank p < 0.001). At 1 and 2 years, PFS rates were 57.6% and 15.2% in patients with sarcopenia versus 84.1% and 56.0% in those without sarcopenia, respectively. In separate multivariable models, CT-defined sarcopenia remained independently associated with shorter PFS (HR, 3.22; 95% CI, 1.86-5.59; p < 0.001), whereas higher continuous SMI (HR, 0.93; 95% CI, 0.89-0.97; p = 0.001) and TMA (HR, 0.97; 95% CI, 0.96-0.99; p = 0.002) were independently associated with longer PFS. Higher Ki-67 expression and second-line CDK4/6 inhibitor therapy also remained significantly associated with shorter PFS across all three models. Conclusions CT-defined sarcopenia was an independent prognostic factor of inferior PFS in patients with HR+/HER2- metastatic breast cancer receiving CDK4/6 inhibitor-based therapy. Assessment of skeletal muscle mass on routinely acquired baseline CT scans may offer a practical tool for risk stratification and may help identify patients requiring more intensive follow-up and supportive care.

In separate multivariable models, CT-defined sarcopenia remained independently associated with shorter PFS (HR, 3.22; 95% CI, 1.86-5.59; p < 0.001), whereas higher continuous SMI (HR, 0.93; 95% CI, 0.89-0.97; p = 0.001) and TMA (HR, 0.97; 95% CI, 0.96-0.99; p = 0.002) were independently associated with longer PFS. Higher Ki-67 expression and second-line CDK4/6 inhibitor therapy also remained significantly associated with shorter PFS across all three models.

Conclusions

CT-defined sarcopenia was an independent prognostic factor of inferior PFS in patients with HR+/HER2- metastatic breast cancer receiving CDK4/6 inhibitor-based therapy. Assessment of skeletal muscle mass on routinely acquired baseline CT scans may offer a practical tool for risk stratification and may help identify patients requiring more intensive follow-up and supportive care.

title: CT imaging biomarkers after neoadjuvant immunotherapy in resectable non-small cell lung cancer: from response assessment to surgical decision-making.
abstract: Neoadjuvant immune checkpoint blockade, usually combined with platinum-based chemotherapy, has improved pathologic response and event-free survival in patients with resectable non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Preoperative assessment remains difficult, however, because radiographic change does not directly represent the amount of residual viable tumor. Immune-cell infiltration, edema, necrosis, granulomatous nodal reactions, and reparative fibrosis may preserve tumor size despite major or complete pathologic response, whereas small viable tumor nests may remain within an apparently fibrotic bed. This Mini Review examines computed tomography (CT) biomarkers after neoadjuvant immunotherapy, focusing on conventional and dual-energy CT, radiomics, delta-radiomics, and deep-learning models. Size-based response criteria are reproducible but insufficient for tissue characterization. Selected, predominantly retrospective studies suggest that temporal models can add information, but transportability and clinical utility remain uncertain. We distinguish four intended uses: pathologic-response prediction, nodal restaging, technical resectability and operative-complexity assessment, and prognosis. Conventional CT informs anatomy and complication assessment; quantitative response models remain investigational. Suspicious new or enlarging nodes warrant tissue confirmation when the result would alter curative surgery. A structured reporting checklist links imaging uncertainty to multidisciplinary action. Imaging biomarkers should complement clinical, pathologic, and molecular data and should not currently be used to omit surgery.

title: Case Report: Synchronous double primary male breast cancer and non-small cell lung cancer: diagnostic confirmation and multidisciplinary management.
abstract: Background Male breast cancer (MBC) is rare, accounting for approximately 1% of all breast cancers. When MBC is diagnosed simultaneously with a second primary lung cancer, treatment planning becomes particularly complex because diagnostic certainty, technical resectability, competing treatment windows, and radiotherapy safety must all be considered. Case presentation We report a 72-year-old man who was synchronously diagnosed with left invasive ductal breast carcinoma and right lower lobe poorly differentiated non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). The breast cancer was staged as pT 3 N 2a M 0 , AJCC 8th edition stage IIIA, with strong ER/PR expression and HER2 nonamplification. The lung lesion was pathologically diagnosed as poorly differentiated NSCLC without definitive glandular, squamous, or neuroendocrine differentiation and was staged as cT 3 N 0 M 0 , AJCC 8th edition stage IIB. Although stage IIB NSCLC is usually evaluated for surgery, this tumor closely involved the right lower lobe pulmonary vessels and bronchial structures, and thoracic surgeons considered upfront radical resection technically unsafe because of the risks of hemorrhage, extended resection, impaired blood supply to the remaining lobes, and loss of pulmonary function. After multidisciplinary team (MDT) discussion, the patient underwent left modified radical mastectomy, adjuvant AC-T chemotherapy, and simultaneous postmastectomy radiotherapy to the left chest wall/regional nodes with definitive radiotherapy to the right lung lesion plus concurrent cisplatin. Imaging shortly after radiotherapy showed marked shrinkage of the right lung lesion, but subsequent CT and liver MRI suggested systemic progression with multiple hepatic lesions. The patient declined liver biopsy, received one cycle of vinorelbine plus cisplatin with Endostar, discontinued further treatment, and died of liver failure in March 2026. Conclusion This case illustrates that therapeutic prioritization in synchronous double primary cancers should not be determined solely by TNM stage or chronological order of diagnosis. Instead, treatment decisions should integrate pathological distinction, tumor biology, anatomical treatability, technical resectability, curative potential, competing treatment windows, and short-term clinical threat. In selected patients, simultaneous postmastectomy radiotherapy and definitive lung radiotherapy may be feasible when supported by MDT consensus, dosimetric review, and close toxicity monitoring.

title: Reconstruction-aware radiomics for risk stratification of subsolid pulmonary nodules: technical evidence, clinical limits, and translation priorities.
abstract: Subsolid pulmonary nodules (SSNs), including pure ground-glass nodules (pGGNs) and part-solid nodules (PSNs), span transient inflammatory abnormalities and adenocarcinoma-spectrum lesions with widely different management implications. This critical narrative review treats CT reconstruction as part of the quantitative biomarker definition and asks whether targeted or high-spatial-resolution reconstruction provides stable, task-specific information beyond standardized thin-section CT. Evidence was synthesized across direct SSN reconstruction-domain studies, technical robustness studies, and clinical prediction studies. Direct imaging studies support improved depiction of selected fine structures, while same-scan GGN evidence demonstrates substantial pixel-size dependence of radiomic features and model composition. However, most clinical models were not evaluated in paired reconstruction domains, external validation with calibration remains uncommon, and no prospective study demonstrating management or patient benefit from reconstruction-aware radiomics in SSNs was identified in the literature reviewed. Persistent pGGNs provide a biological and technical rationale for investigating incremental quantitative information, but greater benefit than in PSNs has not been demonstrated. In PSNs, any model must add value beyond solid-component measurements, consolidation-to-tumor ratio, morphology, and longitudinal growth. Translation therefore requires reconstruction and segmentation robustness testing, strong conventional comparators, external calibration, prespecified thresholds, and prospective decision-linked evaluation. Until such benefit and safety are demonstrated, reconstruction-aware radiomics should remain investigational or confined to governed, domain-checked decision-support pathways.

title: Vision-language foundation models for multimodal medical image understanding and report generation: a narrative review with quantitative synthesis.
abstract: Vision-language foundation models (VLFMs) for medical image understanding have advanced rapidly, yet evidence supporting clinical deployment remains fragmented. This narrative review synthesizes architectures, training paradigms, benchmarks, public datasets, and translation barriers. Drawing on more than 50 original studies published between 2020 and 2025, we provide a structured descriptive comparison rather than a statistical meta-analysis. In a focused audit of 13 representative studies, BLEU/ROUGE was reported by 31% (4/13), RadGraph F1 by 0% (0/13), CheXpert- or CheXbert-derived label evaluation by 46% (6/13), BERTScore by 8% (1/13), human expert evaluation by 31% (4/13), and inference latency or throughput by 0% (0/13). Because datasets, splits, candidate pools, and metrics differ, cross-task results are presented as exploratory benchmark indicators and not as a clinical-readiness scale. The synthesis identifies persistent concerns involving hallucination, limited interpretability, distribution shift, and narrow demographic and geographic coverage. We propose a minimum clinical validation and reporting standard aligned with the distinct purposes of FDA/Health Canada/MHRA and IMDRF Good Machine Learning Practice, the EU AI Act, TRIPOD+AI, and CLAIM, and identify eleven priority research directions. Medical VLFMs are promising, but progress should be judged by source-traceable, clinically grounded, and externally validated evidence.

title: Whole-tumor histogram analysis of non-Gaussian diffusion MRI models combined with clinicopathological indicators for assessing lymph node metastasis in endometrial cancer.
abstract: Objectives To investigate whether whole-tumor histogram features derived from five non-Gaussian diffusion models, combined with clinicopathological factors, are associated with lymph node metastasis (LNM) in endometrial cancer (EC). Methods This prospective study enrolled 73 patients with histologically confirmed EC and known nodal status. All underwent preoperative 3.0T MRI including diffusion-weighted imaging with 16 b-values. Thirteen parametric maps were derived from five non-Gaussian models: intravoxel incoherent motion (IVIM), diffusion kurtosis imaging (DKI), stretched exponential model (SEM), fractional-order calculus (FROC), and continuous time random walk (CTRW). Clinicopathological data were collected, including demographics, comorbidities, serum markers, pathological type, myometrial invasion, cervical involvement, and MRI-based local stage. Clinical, radiomics, and combined logistic regression models were built. Performance was evaluated using AUC, calibration curves, decision curve analysis, and bootstrap analysis of intercept variability. Results LNM was confirmed in 21 of 73 patients. The clinical model achieved an AUC of 0.837, the radiomics model achieved an AUC of 0.856, and the combined model achieved an AUC of 0.924, with 90.5% sensitivity and 82.7% specificity. DeLong tests revealed no significant AUC differences among models ( P = 0.090-0.140). The combined model had the lowest Brier score (0.092) and provided higher net benefit across threshold probabilities of 0.1-0.3. Conclusion Non-Gaussian diffusion histogram parameters, particularly DKI_K_energy, demonstrate potential for predicting LNM in EC. A combined model incorporating DKI_K_energy with age and pathological type shows promise as a potential biomarker for risk stratification.

title: FroHyNet: frozen temporal priors and trainable hypergraph fusion for brain time-series classification.
abstract: Background Functional brain time-series classification is constrained by small clinical cohorts. Handcrafted features are sample-efficient but discard temporal detail; end-to-end networks must estimate many temporal parameters from limited labels; and frozen time-series foundation models reduce that estimation burden but typically encode each channel independently, leaving coordinated activity across brain regions unmodeled. Methods We introduce the Frozen Temporal-Hypergraph Network (FroHyNet), an asymmetric parallel framework that preserves channel-wise temporal representations from a frozen MantisV2 encoder while a trainable spatio-temporal hypergraph branch learns topology-aware spatial corrections. Bottleneck-mix Top-K (BM-TopK) then residual-injects these corrections only along selected channel and latent-feature axes, treating the spatial stream as a selective update rather than a dense overwrite of the temporal representation. We conduct five-fold cross-validation across two functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) and three functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) datasets. Results FroHyNet achieves the best average accuracy and area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve (AUC) among methods evaluated on all five datasets, while keeping the trainable-parameter count well below those of from-scratch temporal networks. Gains are concentrated on fNIRS, with more modest improvements on the smaller fMRI cohorts. Branch ablations indicate dataset-dependent complementarity between the two streams, and fusion ablations on HC-D favor BM-TopK over the evaluated dense and recurrent alternatives.

title: Deep learning-based CT lesion analysis and radiological burden stratification in clinically diagnosed ventilator-associated pneumonia.
abstract: Ventilator associated pneumonia (VAP) is a major complication in the intensive care unit (ICU) and requires objective computed tomography (CT) evaluation. Therefore, this article conducted a retrospective research analysis and developed a multimodal deep learning framework. Firstly, this retrospective study included 512 patients clinically diagnosed with VAP, and then utilized a developed multimodal deep learning framework for voxel-level lesion segmentation, multi-label radiological discovery classification, and radiological burden grading. This framework integrates the anatomical priors of TotalSegmenter, a three-dimensional (3D) Swin UNETR multitasking network, and cross attention fusion of CT features and ventilation parameters. Ultimately, the study showed that the Dice score for internal validation was 0.847, the macroscopic mean area (AUC) under the subject's working characteristic curve was 0.919, and the weighted kappa was 0.826. External validation showed a Dice score of 0.821, with no significant difference between scanner manufacturers. After adjusting for clinical covariates, including acute physiology and chronic health assessment II (APACHE II) scores, there was still a significant correlation between radiation load level and 28 day mortality (hazard ratio [HR] = 2.34, P < 0.001), supporting its potential prognostic relevance.

title: Post-surgical abdominal wall endometriosis: a retrospective cohort study on clinical features, ultrasound accuracy and recurrence.
abstract: Background Abdominal wall endometriosis (AWE) is a rare but clinically significant condition; yet studies about its preoperative assessment and surgical outcomes remain limited. Our study aimed to characterize its clinical presentation, evaluate the utility of preoperative ultrasound, and investigate postoperative recurrence. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 291 AWE patients who underwent surgical resection. Clinical features, ultrasound-surgical concordance, and factors associated with recurrence were assessed. Lesions were classified into Type I (subcutaneous), Type II (fascial/muscular), and Type III (peritoneal) by infiltration depth, with subgroup comparisons across three types. Results Palpable mass (81.8%) and cyclic pain (46.7%) were the predominant symptoms. 99.7% of patients had prior cesarean section (CS), but no significant differences were found between multiple versus single CS groups in infiltration depth ( P = 0.138), maximum diameter ( P = 0.101), or lesion multiplicity ( P = 0.225). Deeper infiltration was associated with older age at diagnosis ( P = 0.030), longer CS-to-diagnosis interval ( P = 0.023), larger lesions ( P < 0.001), more frequent abdominal wall pain ( P = 0.028), fewer palpable masses ( P = 0.037), and higher rates of postoperative complications ( P = 0.002). Preoperative ultrasound agreed well with intraoperative measurements of maximum lesion diameter (ICC=0.872), but its ability to detect myofascial invasion was limited (positive predictive value 88.8%; negative predictive value 44.7%; false-negative rate 22.9%). The overall postoperative recurrence rate was 1.8%. Exploratory Kaplan-Meier analysis suggested a higher recurrence rate in patients with BMI ≥25 kg/m 2 . However, this result should be interpreted with caution given the limited number of recurrence events. Conclusions AWE occurred mostly in women with a history of CS, yet the number of prior CS did not influence lesion characteristics. Deeper infiltration is associated with greater surgical complexity and higher postoperative complication rates. While preoperative ultrasound reliably measures lesion size, its assessment of myofascial invasion remains limited. The observed recurrence rate was low after surgical excision in our cohort.

title: Contrast-enhanced ultrasound-assisted catheter drainage for paravertebral tuberculous abscesses: a retrospective study of procedural safety.
abstract: Background Paravertebral tuberculous abscess is a clinically important complication of spinal tuberculosis and may require image-guided drainage before definitive surgical management. Contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) may improve visualization of abscess vascularity and internal architecture, but its clinical value in catheter drainage for paravertebral tuberculous abscess remains insufficiently defined. Methods This retrospective historical-control study included 67 patients with lumbar spinal tuberculosis complicated by paravertebral tuberculous abscess who underwent ultrasound-guided catheter drainage at Hangzhou Red Cross Hospital between January 2010 and January 2025. Patients were divided into a conventional ultrasound-guided drainage group (Group A, n = 39) and a CEUS-assisted drainage group (Group B, n = 28). Baseline characteristics, postoperative recovery parameters, inflammatory markers, pain scores, clinical outcomes, and drainage-related complications were compared between groups. Results Postprocedural bleeding occurred after 5 of 41 drainage procedures (12.20%) in the conventional ultrasound-guided group and after 0 of 31 procedures (0.00%) in the CEUS-assisted group. Catheter occlusion and pericatheter purulent discharge rates did not differ between groups. Operative time, length of hospital stay, intraoperative blood loss, inflammatory markers, pain scores, cure rate, and recurrence rate also did not differ between groups. Conclusions In this retrospective historical cohort, CEUS-assisted drainage was associated with fewer recorded postprocedural bleeding events and provided additional anatomical information for procedural planning.

Baseline characteristics, postoperative recovery parameters, inflammatory markers, pain scores, clinical outcomes, and drainage-related complications were compared between groups.

Results

Postprocedural bleeding occurred after 5 of 41 drainage procedures (12.20%) in the conventional ultrasound-guided group and after 0 of 31 procedures (0.00%) in the CEUS-assisted group. Catheter occlusion and pericatheter purulent discharge rates did not differ between groups. Operative time, length of hospital stay, intraoperative blood loss, inflammatory markers, pain scores, cure rate, and recurrence rate also did not differ between groups.

Conclusions

In this retrospective historical cohort, CEUS-assisted drainage was associated with fewer recorded postprocedural bleeding events and provided additional anatomical information for procedural planning.

title: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis masquerading as lung cancer with meningeal metastasis: a case report and literature review.
abstract: Background Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) is an anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated small-vessel vasculitis classically presenting with upper and lower respiratory tract and renal involvement. Central nervous system (CNS) involvement in GPA is rare and is highly prone to being misdiagnosed as intracranial tumor metastasis or intracranial infection. Case report We report a 60-year-old female who presented with recurrent headache and conjunctival injection. She had undergone two surgical procedures for "glaucoma" at an outside hospital without headache relief. Upon admission to our hospital, chest CT revealed multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules, highly suspicious for lung cancer; brain MRI showed dural thickening with subdural effusion; lumbar puncture revealed an intracranial pressure (ICP) of 270 mmH₂O, with negative CSF cultures and no tumor cells. The initial diagnosis was leptomeningeal metastasis from lung cancer. However, percutaneous lung biopsy showed no evidence of tumor or infection, and serology revealed positive c-ANCA/PR3-ANCA, leading to a final diagnosis of GPA with clinicoradiologically supported GPA-related pachymeningitis. After glucocorticoid therapy, the patient's headache and other symptoms resolved rapidly. Literature review We reviewed 33 published cases of GPA with cranial involvement and summarized their clinical features. Hypertrophic pachymeningitis (HP) was the most common cranial manifestation (51.5%). Serum ANCA positivity was 87.9% (29/33). Among all 33 cases, c-ANCA/PR3-ANCA was reported in 23 (69.7%); among the 29 ANCA-positive cases, c-ANCA/PR3-ANCA accounted for 79.3% (23/29). After immunosuppressive or immunomodulatory therapy, approximately 90.9% of patients improved or stabilized. These features may serve as clues that should prompt clinicians to consider GPA in the differential diagnosis of pulmonary nodules with pachymeningeal disease and raised intracranial pressure, rather than as established discriminators from lung cancer brain metastasis. Conclusion GPA can present with multiple pulmonary masses, headache, and pachymeningitis, closely mimicking leptomeningeal metastasis of lung cancer. When imaging and clinical presentation are atypical, serum ANCA testing and pathological biopsy are key to differential diagnosis. Clinicians should be alert to this "mimic of malignancy" to avoid unnecessary surgery or radiotherapy.

title: High-frequency ultrasound-derived imaging biomarkers in inflammatory skin diseases.
abstract: Background Inflammatory skin diseases produce structural, vascular, and tissue-remodeling changes that may extend beyond abnormalities detectable by clinical examination. High-frequency ultrasound (HFUS), including ultra-high-frequency systems, provides noninvasive, real-time assessment of cutaneous morphology and inflammatory vascular activity. Objective To examine HFUS in inflammatory skin diseases from an imaging biomarker perspective, emphasizing measurable structural, vascular, and mechanical features and their potential clinical applications. Key findings Candidate ultrasound biomarkers include epidermal and dermal thickness, echogenicity, tissue interfaces, perifollicular abnormalities, fluid collections, fibrosis, architectural distortion, Doppler-detected vascularity, and tissue stiffness. Their clinical relevance is particularly evident in psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, acne vulgaris, hidradenitis suppurativa, and morphea, with emerging applications in other inflammatory dermatoses. In selected disorders, HFUS may reveal clinically occult abnormalities, while treatment-associated changes in selected parameters support their potential as candidate treatment-response biomarkers. Quantitative image analysis, elastography, and artificial intelligence may further improve reproducibility and interpretation. Conclusions HFUS is evolving from predominantly morphological imaging toward a platform for deriving imaging biomarkers in inflammatory skin disease. Broader clinical implementation will require standardized acquisition, validated biomarkers and thresholds, operator training, and prospective evidence demonstrating clinical utility.

title: Guide plate technology improves traditional fluoroscopy on the fixation of AO/OTA 33-C distal femur fractures with integrated nail-plate double distalis entry technique: a retrospective comparative study.
abstract: Introduction NPC (nail-plate construct) has become the surgical mainstay for AO/OTA 33-C-type femoral fracture. Two NPC (nail-plate construct) techniques have been developed: a dedicated surgical guide device-assisted technique (NPC-GD) which adjusts conventional intraoperative fluoroscopy to lead to more accurate reduction of fractures and safer implant placement than ordinary fluoroscopy-guided technique, and a regular fluoroscopy-guided technique (NPC-GF). Aim: Comparison of surgical outcomes, quality of life and functional recovery in patients with AO/OTA 33-C-type femoral fractures using either NPC-GD or NPC-GF. Methods A retrospective comparative analysis was conducted among 161 cases enrolled from Jan. 2020 to Jan. 2025 including 86 cases in NPC-GD group and 75 cases in NPC-GF group. Operative time, operation blood loss, fluoroscopy frequency, rate of malunion, healing time, weight-bearing time, knee range of motion and HSS knee score were statistically compared. Outcome evaluations were all performed in a blinded fashion. Results This final analysis included 161 patients: 86 in the NPC-GD group and 75 in the NPC-GF group. NPC-GD group had a shorter operative time ( P = 0.006), intraoperative ( P = 0.004) and postoperative ( P = 0.003) blood loss, fewer numbers of intraoperative fluoroscopic images ( P = 0.034), shorter time to radiographic fracture union ( P = 0.037), earlier onset of walking at final follow-up ( P = 0.001), earlier achievement of full weight-bearing at final follow-up ( P = 0.009), greater final knee range of motion ( P = 0.009), better HSS knee scores ( P = 0.002). Conclusions NPC-GD is the optimized fluoroscopy technique; it reduces the surgical damage and excess irradiation. NPC-GD can facilitate fracture healing and achieve satisfactory repair of knee function, which is a preferred method of AO/OTA 33-C distal femoral fracture internal fixation.

title: A fatal threat: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia with rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease in anti-MDA5-positive dermatomyositis-a case report.
abstract: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) is a respiratory infection caused by Pneumocystis organisms, representing an opportunistic fungal infection. The clinical occurrence of PJP combined with rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease (RP-ILD) in dermatomyositis (DM) have also been reported occasionally, but patients with this combination of conditions experience rapid disease progression and high mortality rates. We reported a 70-year-old female patient with dyspnea and fever, detailing her laboratory tests, computed tomography (CT) findings and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid findings. The patient's main clinical manifestations were dyspnea and fever. CT scans revealed scattered reticular opacities and ground-glass opacities in both lungs and metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) of the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid detected Pneumocystis jirovecii. Laboratory tests revealed positive anti-MDA5 antibodies during hospitalization. The patient was treated with high-flow oxygen therapy and methylprednisolone upon admission. Subsequently, the patient received mechanical ventilator support and was administered trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX), plasma exchanges and immunoglobulin treatment. The patient's fever subsided, but respiratory failure and interstitial lung disease continued to progressively worsen. Ground-glass opacities, mixed ground-glass opacities, consolidations and reticular opacities were significantly more pronounced than on admission, indicating RP-ILD changes post-treatment. The patient succumbed after 13 days of treatment. PJP complicated by rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease can be fatal in patients, emphasizing the critical importance of early identification of PJP and prompt initiation of anti-PJP treatment. It is crucial to recognize that some MDA5+ DM patients may not present with the typical rash, and in certain cases, RP-ILD may be the primary manifestation. Therefore, early screening for anti-MDA5 antibodies is essential for patients presenting with unexplained early-stage RP-ILD.

title: Beyond overall accuracy: subgroup performance and threshold calibration of AI-assisted chest radiography for equity-oriented pulmonary tuberculosis screening.
abstract: Artificial intelligence-assisted computer-aided detection (CAD) can expand access to chest radiography interpretation for pulmonary tuberculosis screening and triage, but high overall discrimination does not ensure safety at a deployed threshold. This focused narrative Mini Review synthesizes evidence on subgroup performance, threshold calibration, external validity, and implementation of CAD for adult pulmonary tuberculosis. Smear-negative, asymptomatic, and some HIV-associated disease may be less radiographically visible, increasing false-negative risk. Conversely, previous tuberculosis and competing chronic abnormalities reduce specificity and concentrate unnecessary confirmatory testing. Sex, age, geography, clinical setting, verification design, and software version can further alter operating performance. A numerical threshold is therefore not a portable algorithm property but a context-specific clinical resource-allocation policy. We propose a lifecycle in which programs define the intended use, lock the product and version, conduct representative local validation, select an operating point under explicit sensitivity and capacity constraints, audit clinically relevant subgroups, and monitor the complete care pathway. Stratified thresholds and multivariable models may improve selected settings, but current evidence does not justify replacing robust local calibration and governance. Prospective evaluations should compare threshold strategies under common verification standards and report missed cases, referral burden, treatment initiation, and patient-important outcomes.

title: Thyroid-bed schwannoma mimicking a thyroid neoplasm: a case report.
abstract: Intrathyroidal schwannomas are rare, and thyroid-bed schwannomas are scarcer, with merely a few case reports and tough preoperative differentiation. We report a 33-year-old female with a swallowing-movable left neck mass and normal thyroid function. Gray-scale B-mode ultrasound, color Doppler flow imaging and contrast-enhanced ultrasound showed showed a heterogeneously enhanced TI-RADS 3 lesion preoperatively suspected as a follicular neoplasm. Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) biopsy was performed, which failed to yield a definitive pathological diagnosis and yielded Bethesda category I. She received left lobectomy plus isthmectomy, and pathology confirmed thyroid-bed schwannoma sparing thyroid parenchyma; she recovered well with normal thyroid function postoperatively. Due to its low incidence, this tumor is often mistaken for an intrathyroidal nodule on ultrasound. Total surgical excision is the first-line therapy with good overall prognosis. Unlike intrathyroidal schwannomas, most thyroid-bed lesions can be enucleated alone without routine thyroidectomy; hemithyroidectomy is needed for dense adhesion, and total thyroidectomy is rarely required. Considering the low diagnostic value of FNA, multidisciplinary consultation of pathology, radiology and surgery is advised for lesions with atypical imaging, inconclusive FNA or ill-defined thyroid margins. Ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy (CNB) should be performed if needed to tailor proper treatment.

title: Concurrent Bartholin gland and perianal abscesses in a woman: a case report of a diagnostic challenge.
abstract: Background Bartholin gland abscess and perianal abscess are common suppurative infections involving anatomically adjacent regions of the female perineum. Because both conditions may present with localized pain and swelling, distinguishing their respective origins and determining the extent of infection can be challenging. The concomitant occurrence of these two abscesses is uncommon, and its diagnostic and therapeutic considerations remain poorly characterized. We report a rare case of concomitant Bartholin gland and perianal abscesses and describe the diagnostic process and multidisciplinary surgical management. Case presentation An 18-year-old woman presented with progressive perineal and perianal pain and swelling. Pelvic computed tomography demonstrated abscess formation involving the perianal and left perineal soft tissues, and a possible communication between the two lesions was initially suspected. Emergency surgery was performed. The perianal abscess was incised and drained, and an infected anal gland was identified and excised, with bridge drainage established between the drainage incisions. Intraoperative exploration revealed no communication between the perianal abscess and the adjacent perineal lesion. Following gynecological consultation, the separate left vulvar abscess was drained and treated with Jacobi ring fistulization. Culture of the perineal abscess grew Escherichia coli, whereas the perianal abscess culture showed no bacterial growth. Follow-up magnetic resonance imaging 1 month after surgery demonstrated a cystic lesion in the anatomical region of the left Bartholin gland, supporting the Bartholin gland origin of the previously drained perineal abscess. The patient showed satisfactory clinical recovery, with complete healing of the perianal and perineal wounds at 4 months and no evidence of recurrent abscess during the available follow-up. Conclusion Concomitant Bartholin gland and perianal abscesses may be difficult to distinguish because of their overlapping clinical manifestations and anatomical proximity. Clinicians should consider the possibility of multiple independent or potentially related infectious foci and systematically evaluate adjacent anatomical regions. Careful physical examination, appropriate imaging, intraoperative assessment, and timely multidisciplinary collaboration can facilitate accurate diagnosis and individualized surgical management.

title: A nomogram model for preoperative evaluation of invasive degree in lung adenocarcinoma: integrating intratumoral and 2 mm peritumoral radiomics scores with conventional features.
abstract: Objective To determine the optimal peritumoral margin for predicting invasiveness in lung adenocarcinoma and to develop and validate a nomogram integrating conventional CT features with intratumoral and peritumoral radiomics scores for non-invasive preoperative assessment of invasive degree. Methods This retrospective study included 171 patients with pathologically confirmed pulmonary nodules from the Affiliated Hospital of Liaoning University of Traditional Chinese Medicine (January 2018 - December 2025), randomly split into training ( n = 120) and test ( n = 51) sets (7:3 ratio). Based on the 2021 WHO classification, nodules were classified as pre-microinvasive (AAH, AIS, MIA) or invasive (IAC). Conventional CT features and 107 radiomics features were extracted from intratumoral and varying peritumoral margins (0-2, 0-4, 0-6, and 0-8 mm). Feature selection was performed using LASSO and logistic regression to construct five models: a conventional model, an intratumoral radiomics score model, peritumoral radiomics score models (at different margins), an intratumoral-peritumoral radiomics score model, and a combined conventional-intratumoral-peritumoral radiomics model. Performance was assessed via ROC curves, DCA, calibration curves, nested 5-fold cross-validation (25 iterations) and nested Bootstrap (1,000 iterations). Model interpretability was analyzed using SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations). Results Multivariate logistic regression identified maximum diameter and mean CT value as independent predictors. Among the four peritumoral ranges, the 2 mm peritumoral radiomics score model showed optimal performance (AUC: 0.902 training, 0.881 test), establishing 2 mm as the optimal margin. The combined model (conventional + intratumoral + 2 mm peritumoral) achieved the best predictive performance (AUC: 0.925 training, 0.888 test), outperforming the conventional and single radiomics models. The model demonstrated good calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow test, P > 0.05). To prevent information leakage, nested 5-fold cross-validation (25 iterations) and nested Bootstrap (1,000 iterations) were performed on the training set, yielding a mean AUC of 0.873 ± 0.079 and 0.763 (95% CI: 0.572-0.907), respectively. DCA confirmed a favorable net clinical benefit. SHAP analysis identified the intratumoral-2 mm peritumoral radiomics score, mean CT value, and maximum diameter as the top three contributing features. Conclusion A 2 mm peritumoral margin is optimal for predicting lung adenocarcinoma invasiveness. The proposed nomogram enables non-invasive, accurate preoperative prediction with strong interpretability and clinical utility, serving as a reliable tool for guiding individualized surgical planning.

This retrospective study included 171 patients with pathologically confirmed pulmonary nodules from the Affiliated Hospital of Liaoning University of Traditional Chinese Medicine (January 2018 - December 2025), randomly split into training (n = 120) and test (n = 51) sets (7:3 ratio). Conventional CT features and 107 radiomics features were extracted from intratumoral and varying peritumoral margins (0-2, 0-4, 0-6, and 0-8 mm). Multivariate logistic regression identified maximum diameter and mean CT value as independent predictors. The combined model (conventional + intratumoral + 2 mm peritumoral) achieved the best predictive performance (AUC: 0.925 training, 0.888 test), outperforming the conventional and single radiomics models. title: Ultrasound-guided distal versus conventional radial artery catheterization in older surgical patients: protocol for a randomized controlled noninferiority trial.
abstract: Background Invasive radial arterial monitoring is frequently required in older surgical patients, but age-related vascular changes can make catheterization difficult. Distal radial access may improve catheter stability during wrist movement, shorten hemostasis, and preserve the conventional forearm segment; however, its smaller caliber may reduce technical success. This trial will determine whether ultrasound-guided distal radial artery catheterization is noninferior to conventional radial artery catheterization for first-attempt success in patients aged 65 years or older. Materials and methods This single-center, parallel-group, randomized noninferiority trial will enroll 198 surgical patients aged 65 years or older who require invasive arterial pressure monitoring. Participants will be allocated 1:1 to distal or conventional radial artery catheterization. Both groups will receive the same real-time ultrasound-guided dynamic needle-tip positioning technique and a 20G*45 mm catheter; only the access site and limb position will differ. The operator cannot be masked, whereas postoperative outcome assessors and the statistician will be masked where feasible. The primary outcome is first-attempt success, defined as catheter placement with free aspiration and an undamped arterial waveform after one skin puncture. Secondary outcomes are overall assigned-site success, procedural efficiency, intraoperative catheter performance, access-site safety and hemostasis, and Doppler-confirmed arterial patency. Noninferiority will be concluded if the lower limit of the two-sided 95% confidence interval for the risk difference (distal minus conventional) is greater than -15 percentage points in both the intention-to-treat (ITT) and per-protocol (PP) populations. Ethics and dissemination The protocol was prepared in accordance with SPIRIT 2025. This research protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of Ningbo No. 6 Hospital on 12th March 2026 (Approval No.: 2026-10L), and written informed consent will be obtained before randomization. Results will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications and scientific presentations. De-identified data and analysis code will be shared after publication, subject to ethics approval and privacy requirements. Clinical trial registration www.chictr.org.cn; identifier ChiCTR2600124338.

title: Case Report: Distal ureteral obstruction decades after presumed intrauterine device removal in a woman with uterus didelphys.
abstract: Background An ectopic intrauterine device (IUD) can rarely cause ureteral obstruction and hydroureteronephrosis. Diagnosis may be delayed when a prior removal procedure is believed to have been complete. Case presentation A 48-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of right flank pain and urinary frequency after repeated treatment for presumed urinary tract infection and possible genitourinary tuberculosis without sustained improvement. More than 20 years earlier, an IUD had been inserted before uterus didelphys was recognized. Two to three years later, an unintended pregnancy led to recognition of the duplicated uterine anatomy, induced abortion, and an IUD removal procedure. The original records were unavailable, so device location and intact retrieval at that time could not be verified. Multimodality imaging at the index admission showed severe right hydroureteronephrosis, focal distal ureteral narrowing, and an ectopic metallic IUD outside both uterine cavities; cystoscopy was unremarkable. Open ureteral exploration and reconstruction identified an intact IUD with an attached calculus externally compressing an approximately 1-cm fixed distal ureteral stricture without entering the ureteral lumen. The narrowing persisted after device removal, requiring segmental ureteral resection and anastomosis over a double-J stent. Histopathology of the resected ureter showed chronic inflammatory changes without tuberculous changes. The stent was removed 2 months postoperatively. At 6 months after surgery, computed tomography showed marked decompression of the right collecting system and no residual pelvic metallic device; serum creatinine remained normal. Conclusion A history of IUD removal should not be treated as proof of device absence when intact retrieval is undocumented. In otherwise unexplained unilateral ureteral obstruction, a remote IUD history should prompt review of prior device localization and targeted pelvic imaging, particularly when historical records are unavailable or duplicated uterine anatomy complicates localization. A fixed stricture may require reconstruction even after the ectopic device is removed.

title: EUS-guided targeted epinephrine injection and immediate intraoperative bleeding during endoscopic mucosal resection: a retrospective cohort study (with video).
abstract: Objective To investigate whether endoscopic ultrasound (EUS)-guided targeted epinephrine injection is associated with a lower rate of bleeding during endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR). Methods This retrospective cohort study enrolled consecutive patients undergoing EMR for gastrointestinal lesions ≥1 cm with an EUS-detectable feeding vessel at Zhengzhou Central Hospital between January 2025 and March 2026. Patients were non-randomly assigned to EUS-guided targeted epinephrine injection (1:20,000) or EUS assessment followed by conventional submucosal saline injection. The primary outcome was immediate intraoperative bleeding; secondary outcomes included delayed bleeding, procedure time, hospital stay, en bloc resection rate, and adverse events. Multivariable logistic regression was performed, with Firth regression and propensity-score (PSM and IPTW) sensitivity analyses to address confounding. Results Among 84 patients (injection group, n = 31; control group, n = 53), immediate intraoperative bleeding occurred in 0% versus 24.5% ( P = 0.002). Two delayed bleeding cases (3.8%) occurred in the control group only. No between-group differences were observed in procedure time, hospital stay, or adverse events; the en bloc resection rate was 100% in both groups. EUS-guided targeted epinephrine injection was associated with reduced odds of intraoperative bleeding (OR = 0.112, 95% CI 0.028-0.443, P = 0.002), consistent across Firth regression, PSM, and IPTW analyses. Conclusion EUS-guided targeted epinephrine injection was associated with lower immediate intraoperative bleeding during EMR without prolonging procedure time or hospital stay. These hypothesis-generating findings require confirmation in prospective randomized studies.

title: Case Report: Pulmonary benign metastasizing leiomyoma diagnosed through clinicopathological correlation.
abstract: Background Pulmonary benign metastasizing leiomyoma (PBML) is a rare condition characterized by histologically benign smooth-muscle tumors involving the lung, typically in women with a history of uterine leiomyoma. Its radiological features are nonspecific and may overlap with primary pulmonary neoplasms, metastatic malignancies, and other mesenchymal lesions. Diagnosis therefore depends on clinicopathological correlation integrating pulmonary pathological findings with the relevant gynecologic history. Case presentation A 47-year-old woman with a history of uterine leiomyoma underwent evaluation for two right pulmonary nodules detected approximately 6 years and 8 months after uterine myomectomy. Follow-up CT showed stability of the right upper lobe nodule and slight enlargement of the right middle lobe nodule. Thoracoscopic wedge resections were performed for definitive diagnosis. Intraoperative frozen-section examination yielded different provisional interpretations for the two lesions and did not establish a definitive diagnosis. Permanent histopathological examination demonstrated spindle-cell tumors with smooth-muscle differentiation and hormone-receptor expression. Further clarification of the patient's remote gynecologic history, together with the pulmonary morphology and immunophenotype, supported the diagnosis of PBML. At the 1-month postoperative follow-up, no evidence of recurrence was identified, and annual CT surveillance was planned. Conclusion PBML should be considered in the differential diagnosis of pulmonary nodules in women with a current or remote history of uterine leiomyoma. When pulmonary spindle-cell morphology is not diagnostic in isolation, integration of gynecologic history, imaging findings, permanent histopathology, and immunohistochemical findings is important for accurate diagnosis and avoidance of misclassification. This case highlights the value of clinicopathological communication when evaluating pulmonary mesenchymal lesions.

title: Twenty-six years of misdiagnosis as gastroesophageal reflux disease in a patient with achalasia presenting with chronic dysphagia: a case report.
abstract: Impaired relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter and absent peristalsis throughout the esophageal body constitute the core pathological manifestations of achalasia. High-resolution manometry is rarely accessible at primary medical institutions. Coupled with substantial overlap between its clinical manifestations and gastroesophageal reflux disease, missed diagnosis and prolonged misdiagnosis occur frequently. This report describes a 70-year-old male patient afflicted with progressive dysphagia for as long as 26 years. Repeated esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) misclassified his complaint as gastroesophageal reflux disease, and proton pump inhibitors only relieved symptoms transiently. His clinical status deteriorated drastically over the past three months, accompanied by a 5-kilogram weight loss. Combining typical clinical history, chest computed tomography, EGD and the pathognomonic bird-beak deformity observed on upper gastrointestinal barium swallow, a clinical diagnosis of achalasia was established. His initial Eckardt score was 8. The patient received peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM) without intraoperative complications, and his dysphagia resolved rapidly after surgery. No symptom relapse was recorded in the 6-month postoperative follow-up. His body weight recovered by 4 kg, and the follow-up Eckardt score dropped to 0. This case delivers critical clinical implications. Clinicians tend to confuse achalasia with gastroesophageal reflux disease, and short-term symptomatic improvement induced by proton pump inhibitors may potentially mask the underlying disease and contribute to diagnostic delay. When high-resolution manometry cannot be performed, a definitive diagnosis can be reached through typical medical history, barium radiography and EGD evaluation. POEM delivers satisfying safety profiles and prominent short-term efficacy for patients suffering from long-standing achalasia.

title: Case Report: Durable, well-tolerated complete response to epcoritamab plus pirtobrutinib in Richter transformation relapsing after CD19 CAR T-cell therapy.
abstract: Richter transformation (RT) that relapses after CD19-directed chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has no established therapy and carries a dismal prognosis. We report an 84-year-old man with multiply relapsed, biopsy-proven diffuse large B-cell lymphoma-type RT and a high-risk MYC/BCL2 double-expressor phenotype who developed systemic relapse, with extensive osteolytic bone disease, after lisocabtagene maraleucel. Three cycles of atezolizumab produced no objective benefit. Treatment with epcoritamab, a CD3xCD20 bispecific antibody, plus pirtobrutinib, a non-covalent Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor, produced complete nodal metabolic resolution within 3 months that deepened to a complete metabolic response (Deauville score 2) by 10 treatment cycles, with resolution of two interim osteolytic lesions whose transient nature illustrates the interpretive challenges of PET/CT response assessment after cellular and T-cell-engaging therapies. The chemotherapy-free regimen was well tolerated at age 84, with no cytokine release syndrome, no neurotoxicity, and no cytopenias; the only toxicity was mild, reversible dexamethasone-related myopathy. The patient remains in ongoing clinical remission after approximately 10 months of therapy. This case extends the reported experience with epcoritamab plus pirtobrutinib specifically to the post-CAR T-cell relapse setting and suggests that this chemotherapy-free doublet may warrant consideration as a salvage strategy for older or frail patients with RT who are unfit for further cytotoxic therapy.

title: Latest observed volumetric MRI response and lesion level local control after gamma knife radiosurgery for breast cancer brain metastases.
abstract: Background Serial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reveals heterogeneous lesion responses after stereotactic radiosurgery beyond binary local-control status. We characterized latest-observed volumetric response categories after Gamma Knife radiosurgery (GKRS) for breast cancer brain metastases and examined their concordance with 12-month local control (LC 12 m). Methods This retrospective study included 80 patients, 182 lesions, and 819 MRI records. LC 12 m incorporated earlier local failure or assessment within a 10-14-month window. Four response categories compared the latest eligible whole-tumor (WT) volume with baseline. Baseline imaging and dose correlates of failure were evaluated using variational Bayesian mixed-effects logistic regression and patient-clustered generalized estimating equations (GEE). Early-landmark analyses explored associations with subsequent failure. Results LC 12 m was evaluable in 105/182 lesions (70 controlled, 35 failed). Among 154 response-classifiable lesions, 24 (15.6%) showed complete response, 56 (36.4%) partial regression, 48 (31.2%) stable volume, and 26 (16.9%) enlargement. Enlargement was strongly associated with failure (GEE odds ratio 16.797, 95% confidence interval 3.398-83.033). Contemporaneous concordance measures were 54.3% sensitivity, 97.1% specificity, 90.5% positive predictive value, and 81.0% negative predictive value; 97/105 category assessments occurred within the endpoint window. Early-landmark analyses were inconclusive. In 102 complete cases, variational Bayesian odds ratios were 1.888 [95% credible interval (CrI): 1.079-3.302] per unit increase in ln[1 + WT (cm 3 )], 3.071 (1.520-6.203) for edema, and 0.760 (0.697-0.829) per 10-Gy increase in BED 10 . GEE estimates were directionally consistent but did not reach statistical significance. Same-model, same-prior Markov chain Monte Carlo analysis supported the inverse association between BED 10 and local failure, whereas evidence for the WT and edema associations remained inconclusive. Conclusions Serial volumetric MRI and latest-observed response categories complement binary local-control assessment by describing heterogeneous lesion-level responses after GKRS. Enlargement showed strong contemporaneous concordance with LC 12 m, with overlapping definitions and assessment times limiting claims of independent prediction. Baseline imaging and BED 10 associations were model-dependent. External validation is needed to establish the framework's added clinical value.

In 102 complete cases, variational Bayesian odds ratios were 1.888 [95% credible interval (CrI): 1.079-3.302] per unit increase in ln[1 + WT (cm3)], 3.071 (1.520-6.203) for edema, and 0.760 (0.697-0.829) per 10-Gy increase in BED10. GEE estimates were directionally consistent but did not reach statistical significance. Same-model, same-prior Markov chain Monte Carlo analysis supported the inverse association between BED10 and local failure, whereas evidence for the WT and edema associations remained inconclusive.

Conclusions

Serial volumetric MRI and latest-observed response categories complement binary local-control assessment by describing heterogeneous lesion-level responses after GKRS. Enlargement showed strong contemporaneous concordance with LC12m, with overlapping definitions and assessment times limiting claims of independent prediction. Baseline imaging and BED10 associations were model-dependent. External validation is needed to establish the framework's added clinical value.

title: Medial repair band: independent risk factor for collapse in traumatic osteonecrosis of the femoral head.
abstract: Objective Femoral head collapse is closely associated with a poor prognosis in osteonecrosis of the femoral head (ONFH). This study aimed to evaluate the association between the MRI repair band and the progression to collapse in traumatic osteonecrosis of the femoral head (TONFH). Methods We retrospectively analyzed TONFH patients admitted from January 2016 to May 2023. The following clinical data were collected: patient age, sex, affected side, presence of complete fracture displacement, performance of emergency surgery, achievement of anatomical reduction, and other relevant clinical characteristics. Median follow-up was 44.5 months, with collapse >2 mm as the survival endpoint. Univariate and multivariate regression analyses assessed the association between MRI medial repair band and collapse. Inter-observer consistency was evaluated using Kappa test. We also analyzed the association between fracture displacement and MRI medial repair band. Results 148 TONFH patients were included [median age 46.50 years (IQR: 38.50-52.00); 67(45.27%) males, 81(54.73%) females]. Collapse occurred in 63 (collapse group) vs. 85 (non-collapse group). The interobserver reliability of the medial repair zone, as measured by the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), was 0.802.Multivariate analysis identified the medial repair band as an independent risk factor for collapse (OR: 13.350, 95% CI: 5.767-30.907; P < 0.001). Survival was significantly lower with a medial vs. lateral repair band ( P < 0.001). Garden type IV fracture was significantly associated with medial repair band formation (OR: 2.581, 95% CI: 1.304-5.106; P = 0.006). Conclusion The medial repair band on MRI is an independent risk factor for collapse in patients with TONFH; furthermore, Garden type IV is closely associated with the formation of the medial repair band. The MRI medial repair band is an imaging feature for assessing the risk of collapse in TONFH.

title: Computed tomography-derived bone and muscle biomarkers after fragility hip fracture: readiness for precision risk stratification.
abstract: Fragility hip fracture is heterogeneous in local skeletal competence, physiological reserve, and recovery potential. Computed tomography (CT), when already acquired for clinical care, can provide proximal-femoral attenuation or quantitative CT-derived bone mineral density, muscle cross-sectional area, and composition metrics. This Mini Review separates acute fracture-status discrimination, pre-fracture longitudinal prediction, and post-index-fracture prognostication. Local femoral attenuation has been associated with fixation-related complications, but it is an indirect structural marker whose interpretation depends on geometry, loading, reduction, and implant-bone interactions. Muscle composition can complement size, but neither directly measures force, coordination, or functional performance. High apparent discrimination frequently derives from the development sample; evidence of added value over clinical predictors, calibration, and independent validation remains limited. We organize interpretation by anatomy, metric, outcome, and time, and illustrate how structural imaging could be combined with clinical, functional, and biomechanical measurements for four post-fracture endpoints. This is an endpoint-specific evidence interpretation framework, not a validated prediction model or treatment algorithm. Prognostic enrichment must be distinguished from treatment-effect modification. Harmonized measurements, external validation, and prospective evaluation of biomarker-guided decisions are required before these phenotypes can support individualized interventions.

title: Early radiology reports and ECG machine measurements do not measurably improve 30-day ICU mortality prediction from the first 6 h of the stay: a multimodal ablation with external validation of the structured EHR backbone.
abstract: Whether electrocardiographic measurements and unstructured clinical notes add prognostic information to structured electronic health records for early ICU mortality prediction remains unresolved. We trained a modality-attention model on tabular EHR features, machine-derived ECG measurements, printed diagnostic statements, and biomedical language-model representations of notes, all drawn from the first 6 h after ICU admission. Within that window, the only usable text in MIMIC-IV is the radiology report, available for 19.6% of stays. The discharge summary is the only other free-text table, but in 98.6% of stays in which it was charted during the window, it was filed after the window had closed. Mortality was assessed at 48 h, 7 days, and 30 days after ICU admission, with 30 days as the primary endpoint. The 6-h window is the period from which the predictors are drawn, not the interval over which death is predicted. Post-window features, including total ICU length of stay, were excluded. The cohort comprised each adult's first ICU stay in MIMIC-IV v3.1 (65,366 stays), holding out 9,806 (30-day mortality 10.6%), without a minimum stay to avoid day-one survival conditioning. Five variants used five seeds per horizon. EHR-only AUROCs were 0.9371, 0.9106, and 0.8969. Adding ECG, text, or both produced no reliable improvement: at 30 days, every paired AUPRC difference included zero, and the largest gain compatible with the data, 0.0068, was of the order of the study's own training noise. These are confidence limits, not equivalence bounds. No defect was identified in the preprocessing checks performed on the ECG matrix, and the matrix's highest-ranked input still ranked 106th of 1,827. L2-penalized logistic regression reached 0.8844, and the matched architecture added 0.0126 AUROC (0.0083-0.0168). All learned models outperformed SOFA at 0.731 and SAPS-II at 0.793, with DeLong p below 10 ⁻⁵⁹ . Transferred without retraining, the models reached AUROC 0.833 on HiRID, 0.774 on MC-MED, and 0.7268 on eICU-CRD; none of these cohorts supplied ECG or notes, so they tested the structured backbone with both extra modalities masked, and the HiRID and MC-MED 30-day outcomes are derived from length of stay. Mean calibration gaps concealed over-prediction up to 0.167 in the highest-risk decile. AUROC was 0.853 for individuals aged 80 or above; race-stratified AUROC remained 0.878-0.914 compared with 0.897 overall. These findings pertain to early radiology reports and ECG summaries within a 6-h window.

title: MammoDiff: weakly supervised mammographic anomaly detection via classifier-guided denoising diffusion models-a real-world clinical study on the KHCC mammography cohort.
abstract: Introduction Early detection of malignant mammographic lesions is a critical clinical challenge, particularly where large annotated datasets are unavailable. Supervised deep learning achieves near-radiologist performance but requires large datasets with reliable labels and pixel/ROI annotations. Weakly supervised anomaly detection, requiring only image-level binary labels, offers an annotation-efficient alternative, yet prior GAN- and autoencoder-based methods have struggled to preserve fine anatomical detail in the mammographic domain. Methods We present MammoDiff, to our knowledge the first application of classifier-guided denoising diffusion models to weakly supervised mammographic anomaly detection, trained and evaluated on 3,013 mammograms from 806 patients at King Hussein Cancer Center (KHCC), Jordan. MammoDiff encodes input anatomy through deterministic DDIM noise encoding and reconstructs a counterfactual healthy image guided by the gradient signal of a noise-conditioned binary classifier. The anomaly map is the pixel-wise absolute difference between input and reconstruction, and the image-level score is obtained by spatial mean pooling. A 3 × 3 ablation over noise level L ∈ {250, 500, 750} and gradient scale s ∈ {50, 100, 200} was performed on the validation set. Results The optimal configuration ( L = 750, s = 50) achieved AUROC = 0.7246 [95% CI: 0.6685, 0.7825] on the held-out test set ( n = 304), compared with a simplified PatchCore-style baseline (AUROC = 0.6634) and a supervised ResNet-50 reference (AUROC = 0.8100), without pixel-level annotation. The proposed Healthy-Shift Index (HSI) was positive for 94.8% of malignant and 87.4% of normal cases, so it is the separation between the class distributions rather than the sign of the index that carries information. Discussion This performance is not clinically deployable: at the Youden-optimal threshold the sensitivity is 0.6013, meaning that 61 of 153 malignant cases are missed, well below the approximately 87% targeted by FDA-cleared triage devices, and the study is single-centre without external validation. MammoDiff is therefore presented as a methodological proof-of-concept and a reproducible baseline for future work, not as a screening or triage tool..

title: A technical review of dynamic brain functional imaging combined with EEG spectral parameters in the screening of early-stage brain injury.
abstract: Background Early-stage brain injury encompasses subtypes such as mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI), silent stroke and subclinical brain injury. It is characterised by negative imaging findings, subtle symptoms and a high risk of long-term neurological deficits, presenting a key challenge in the early screening and prevention of neurological diseases. Traditional imaging techniques, such as structural Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and Computed Tomography (CT), can only identify organic morphological lesions. Their detection rate for early micro-injuries at the level of neuronal electrophysiology and brain network function is extremely low. Consequently, these techniques struggle to meet the clinical needs for early screening, assessment, and intervention. Methods Electroencephalography (EEG) spectral changes (including conventional spectral slowing and 1/f aperiodic abnormalities) and large-scale dynamic neural network disruption across the entire brain are core pathological features of early brain functional damage; they may serve as indirect correlates of microscopic pathological changes such as an imbalance in neuronal excitation-inhibition and abnormalities in the efficiency of brain information transmission. Based on this, this paper proposes a Dynamic-Spectral Coupling (DSC) framework, which proposes spectral abnormalities as a potential upstream mechanism associated with network reorganisation. Within this framework, this narrative review summarizes dynamic functional magnetic resonance imaging (dynamic fMRI), EEG spectral analysis and multimodal fusion technologies, with a particular focus on elucidating the coupling mechanisms between EEG periodic and 1/f aperiodic spectral parameters and dynamic brain network indicators. Results The review outlines the screening value and application advantages of multimodal fusion technologies in mTBI, occult cerebrovascular injury and subclinical brain injury. Furthermore, the paper summarises the current limitations of these technologies in terms of clinical translation, methodology and database development. Conclusions Taking into account the clinical needs of neurorehabilitation, it proposes future development directions, including the development of lightweight devices, AI-assisted diagnosis, the establishment of standardised analytical systems and the translation of precision rehabilitation. The aim is to provide technical guidance and theoretical support for screening, risk stratification and rehabilitation planning in early-stage brain injury, while acknowledging that clinical utility remains to be established.

title: CT-based prediction of EGFR mutation subtypes and TP53 co-mutation status in lung adenocarcinoma.
abstract: Background Epidermal growth factor receptor ( EGFR ) mutation status is a key determinant of targeted treatment in lung adenocarcinoma, whereas co-occurring TP53 alterations may further affect therapeutic response and prognosis. This study aimed to develop a noninvasive CT-based approach for predicting EGFR mutation subtypes and TP53 co-mutation status in lung adenocarcinoma, thereby providing imaging support for pretreatment risk stratification and clinical decision-making. Methods Patients with pathologically confirmed lung adenocarcinoma who underwent pretreatment chest CT and molecular testing were retrospectively enrolled from a single-center cohort. A total of 1,633 patients were included and categorized into five molecular groups: EGFR wild type, EGFR 19del, EGFR L858R, EGFR 19del with TP53 co-mutation, and EGFR L858 R with TP53 co-mutation. Based on chest CT images, key slice extraction, lesion ROI generation, automatic segmentation, and image standardization were performed. Semantic CT features, radiomics features, and deep CT representations were then derived. Under a unified data partitioning and standardized evaluation framework, four models were constructed and compared for the five-class classification task: a random forest model based on semantic CT features, a support vector machine model based on radiomics features, a Qwen-based semantic classification model, and a MedicalDINOv3-based deep learning model. To eliminate confounding bias induced by multimodal feature fusion, two ablation experiments were supplemented to split the model input features, and two MedicalDINOv3 models were built with inputs restricted to semantic features only and CT images only, respectively. Model performance was assessed using accuracy, macro-averaged area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), and macro-F1 score. External validation was further conducted using public and multicenter datasets. Results Among the 1,633 patients in the internal cohort, 731 were EGFR wild type, 295 had EGFR 19del, 399 had EGFR L858R, 118 had EGFR 19del with TP53 co-mutation, and 90 had EGFR L858 R with TP53 co-mutation. To quantify the independent predictive value of different input modalities, ablation experiments on three variants of MedicalDINOv3 were performed. Ablation results revealed distinct performance among three input strategies. The MedicalDINOv3 with only semantic input obtained a test accuracy of 31.55% and an AUC of 0.6305 with limited predictive ability. The branch solely fed with CT images reached an accuracy of 55.61% and a macro-average AUC of 0.6347. The complete MedicalDINOv3 integrating CT deep features, clinical and semantic features performed best, with a test accuracy of 0.6905 and a macro-average AUC of 0.8788. This comparison proved that CT deep representations outperform traditional handcrafted imaging and semantic features, and multi-modal fusion further improves subtype stratification performance. The support vector machine model achieved an accuracy of 0.527, a macro-AUC of 0.792 and a macro-F1 score of 0.524; the random forest model achieved an accuracy of 0.455, a macro-AUC of 0.819 and a macro-F1 score of 0.412; and the Qwen-based model achieved an accuracy of 0.339, a macro-AUC of 0.700 and a macro-F1 score of 0.316. Receiver operating characteristic analyses showed that the deep learning model provided relatively stable discrimination for EGFR wild type and TP53 co-mutated categories, whereas overlap remained between the two major EGFR -sensitive subtypes, EGFR 19del and EGFR L858 R. In external validation, the public dataset used for EGFR binary classification yielded an overall accuracy of 67.0% and an AUC of 0.6666. The raw overall accuracy of the cohort was 75.5%, and raw overall accuracy is prone to overestimation when the cohort has severe class imbalance dominated by EGFR wild-type samples, which can only serve as an auxiliary reference. Multicenter five-class external validation yielded a balanced accuracy of 58.2% and a macro F1 of 0.574. The subtype-specific AUCs for EGFR wild type, EGFR 19del, EGFR L858R, EGFR 19del with TP53 co-mutation, and EGFR L858 R with TP53 co-mutation were 0.8342, 0.6504, 0.7221, 0.6586, and 0.7563, respectively. Conclusion A CT-based deep learning model can provide noninvasive stratification of EGFR mutation subtypes and TP53 co-mutation status in lung adenocarcinoma. Compared with semantic CT features and radiomics features, deep CT representations showed superior overall discriminative performance. This approach may serve as an adjunctive tool to molecular testing for pretreatment assessment in lung adenocarcinoma. However, the model showed inconsistent generalization performance across different molecular subtypes, with notably limited predictive efficacy for EGFR 19del and EGFR 19del+TP53 subtypes. Therefore, predictions for these categories should be interpreted with caution, and the model requires further validation in larger, multicenter, and standardized datasets before clinical application.

Semantic CT features, radiomics features, and deep CT representations were then derived. Under a unified data partitioning and standardized evaluation framework, four models were constructed and compared for the five-class classification task: a random forest model based on semantic CT features, a support vector machine model based on radiomics features, a Qwen-based semantic classification model, and a MedicalDINOv3-based deep learning model. To eliminate confounding bias induced by multimodal feature fusion, two ablation experiments were supplemented to split the model input features, and two MedicalDINOv3 models were built with inputs restricted to semantic features only and CT images only, respectively. Model performance was assessed using accuracy, macro-averaged area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), and macro-F1 score. External validation was further conducted using public and multicenter datasets.

Results

Among the 1,633 patients in the internal cohort, 731 were EGFR wild type, 295 had EGFR 19del, 399 had EGFR L858R, 118 had EGFR 19del with TP53 co-mutation, and 90 had EGFR L858 R with TP53 co-mutation. To quantify the independent predictive value of different input modalities, ablation experiments on three variants of MedicalDINOv3 were performed. Ablation results revealed distinct performance among three input strategies. The MedicalDINOv3 with only semantic input obtained a test accuracy of 31.55% and an AUC of 0.6305 with limited predictive ability. The branch solely fed with CT images reached an accuracy of 55.61% and a macro-average AUC of 0.6347. The complete MedicalDINOv3 integrating CT deep features, clinical and semantic features performed best, with a test accuracy of 0.6905 and a macro-average AUC of 0.8788. This comparison proved that CT deep representations outperform traditional handcrafted imaging and semantic features, and multi-modal fusion further improves subtype stratification performance. The support vector machine model achieved an accuracy of 0.527, a macro-AUC of 0.792 and a macro-F1 score of 0.524; the random forest model achieved an accuracy of 0.455, a macro-AUC of 0.819 and a macro-F1 score of 0.412; and the Qwen-based model achieved an accuracy of 0.339, a macro-AUC of 0.700 and a macro-F1 score of 0.316. Receiver operating characteristic analyses showed that the deep learning model provided relatively stable discrimination for EGFR wild type and TP53 co-mutated categories, whereas overlap remained between the two major EGFR-sensitive subtypes, EGFR 19del and EGFR L858 R. In external validation, the public dataset used for EGFR binary classification yielded an overall accuracy of 67.0% and an AUC of 0.6666. The raw overall accuracy of the cohort was 75.5%, and raw overall accuracy is prone to overestimation when the cohort has severe class imbalance dominated by EGFR wild-type samples, which can only serve as an auxiliary reference. Multicenter five-class external validation yielded a balanced accuracy of 58.2% and a macro F1 of 0.574. The subtype-specific AUCs for EGFR wild type, EGFR 19del, EGFR L858R, EGFR 19del with TP53 co-mutation, and EGFR L858 R with TP53 co-mutation were 0.8342, 0.6504, 0.7221, 0.6586, and 0.7563, respectively.

Conclusion

A CT-based deep learning model can provide noninvasive stratification of EGFR mutation subtypes and TP53 co-mutation status in lung adenocarcinoma. Compared with semantic CT features and radiomics features, deep CT representations showed superior overall discriminative performance. This approach may serve as an adjunctive tool to molecular testing for pretreatment assessment in lung adenocarcinoma. However, the model showed inconsistent generalization performance across different molecular subtypes, with notably limited predictive efficacy for EGFR 19del and EGFR 19del+TP53 subtypes. Therefore, predictions for these categories should be interpreted with caution, and the model requires further validation in larger, multicenter, and standardized datasets before clinical application.
